issues.subcategory: Overstated synthesis of cognitive interview evidence in Introduction
issues.description: Overstated synthesis of cognitive interview evidence in Introduction: The synthesis of the cognitive-interview evidence is internally muddled. The preceding paragraph says cognitive interview has not been shown to eliminate memory conformity and that cognitive-interview/Self-Administered Interview findings in the classic misinformation paradigm are quite inconsistent, but the next sentence summarizes cognitive interview as “not effective” for memory conformity and appears to imply that it was effective in the classic misinformation context.
issues.quote:
The third technique that has been analyzed in the context of memory conformity is cognitive interview (Geiselman, 1984; Ginet et al., 2019), but its effectiveness in eliminating the memory conformity effect has not been demonstrated. In the context of the classic misinformation effect, the results concerning cognitive interview and a related technique, Self-Administered Interview, have been quite inconsistent (Centofanti and Reece, 2006; Gabbert, Hope, Fisher, \& Jamieson, 2012; Holliday and Albon, 2004; Holliday et al., 2012; Paterson, Eijkemans, \& Kemp, 2015; LaPaglia et al., 2014).

In view of the aforementioned studies, it is impossible to unequivocally indicate a technique that is effective in reducing the memory conformity effect: warning produced inconsistent results, while cognitive interview and reinforced self-affirmation were not effective (although they were effective in the context of the classic misinformation effect).

issues.subcategory: Contradiction regarding 'extended warning' novelty
issues.description: Contradiction regarding 'extended warning' novelty: The novelty rationale for the extended-warning condition is under-specified: the Introduction has just cited Cadavid and Luna (2021) as finding that an “extensive warning” reduced memory conformity, so describing an “extended warning” as one of “three new ways” based mainly on length, detail, and breadth creates ambiguity unless the proposed manipulation is distinguished from that prior extensive warning.
issues.quote: Therefore, in the present paper we decided to explore three new ways of reducing the memory conformity effect: (1) extended warning (which in intention is different from the warnings usually applied in existing research as regards its length, detail and breadth); (2) providing detailed knowledge about the fallibility of memory; (3) demonstrating the vulnerability of memory and motivating participants to overcome it.

issues.subcategory: Normative influence is dismissed too quickly in the rationale
issues.description: Normative influence is dismissed too quickly in the rationale: The rationale may understate normative influence: although the final memory test is individual, misinformation is introduced during a collaborative discussion in which participants compare answers and may experience pressure to agree. Normative yielding during that phase could carry over to the final report, so treating normative impact as having little relevance may make the intervention rationale too narrowly informational.
issues.quote: Given the fact that the individual memory test does not include any element of direct interpersonal pressure, we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect has little use in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is little cost of disagreeing (although it is still possible that some pressure exists as the participant knows that their answers will be reviewed by the experimenter).

issues.subcategory: Premature dismissal of normative influence
issues.description: Premature dismissal of normative influence: The passage may underplay a downstream social-consistency route: participants who yield during the collaborative recall phase may later repeat that answer on the private test to remain consistent with their prior public response. Final-test privacy therefore does not by itself rule out normative or social-motivational contributions to the observed conformity effect.

issues.subcategory: Targeting discrepancy-aware participants is not operationalized
issues.description: Targeting discrepancy-aware participants is not operationalized: The theoretical rationale makes discrepancy awareness central to the proposed mechanism, and later states that the methods should be more effective among participants aware of discrepancies than among those unaware. The analysis plan, however, does not define a discrepancy-awareness measure or planned moderator test. The disputed/non-disputed discussion coding may be informative, but it is not equivalent to individual awareness of a conflict between one’s own memory and the partner’s report.
issues.quote: This, naturally, relates only to participants who are aware of the inconsistencies between the event and the content of the answers provided by the co-witness. In other words, we are speaking about participants who correctly monitor both the source of information and its content. Such participants may choose one of two options: answer in accordance with what they themselves remember about the event (this would be the correct answer) or base their answers on what their partner said (which happens to be the wrong answer).

issues.subcategory: Present-study overview seems to skip the intervention phase
issues.description: Present-study overview seems to skip the intervention phase: The present-study overview describes the MORI sequence as moving from film viewing to discussion and then, “Finally,” to the individual memory test, without mentioning the intervention phase that later occurs between discussion and the test. Because the paragraph begins “In the present experiment,” this gives a locally misleading sequence even though the Method section later clarifies the intended design.
issues.quote:
In the present experiment, the innovative MORI technique (Manipulation of Overlapping Rivalrous Images; Mori, 2003,
2007) will be used to examine memory conformity. The MORI technique enables the simultaneous projection of two movie versions on the same screen. Each of the versions differs in terms of certain details, e.g., in one version the criminal checks the time on a wristwatch while in the other does so on a wall clock. Thanks to polarized glasses (which resemble ordinary sunglasses) that are worn by the pair of participants, each of them sees a different movie version while being convinced that they are actually watching the same movie clip. Thus, the participants sit beside each other, look at the same screen, and are not aware that the other person is watching a different version. After watching the movie, the participants discuss half of the dissimilar details they have seen, therefore they introduce mutual misinformation. Finally, the participants complete the individual memory test to compare the correctness of the answers to the questions about the discussed details (related to misinformation) with the correctness of the answers to the questions about the non-discussed details.

issues.subcategory: Confound in Extended Warning operationalization
issues.description: Confound in Extended Warning operationalization: The Extended warning condition appears to include a source-specific enlightenment that the partner saw a different version of the movie, whereas the Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation conditions do not. This does not necessarily invalidate a comparison of intervention packages, but it makes Extended warning much more diagnostically informative about the source of the discrepancy and complicates both interpretation of between-method differences and the prediction that Demonstration and motivation will be more effective.
issues.quote: The main goal of this proposal is to analyze the efficacy of three possible methods of reducing memory conformity. These are (1) Extended warning against misinformation, (2) providing detailed knowledge about the fallibility of memory (we called this method Education about memory), and (3) demonstrating the vulnerability of memory and motivating subjects to overcome it (called Demonstration and motivation). Each method will be applied in a different group of subjects; the fourth group will be the control.

issues.subcategory: Unmeasured awareness moderator in Section 1.1.1
issues.description: Unmeasured awareness moderator in Section 1.1.1: The theoretical rationale makes awareness of discrepancies a predicted moderator of intervention efficacy, but the protocol does not clearly operationalize individual awareness of the original detail, the partner’s discrepant detail, and their source conflict. The planned outcome indices and confidence ratings can test overall reductions in conformity, but they do not by themselves distinguish awareness from exposure, final accuracy, guessing, or memory distortion; the later disputed/non-disputed coding is also only an imperfect behavioral proxy unless its role is specified more clearly.
issues.quote: From the above reasoning it follows that our methods of reducing the memory conformity effect are directed towards the participants who are aware of the discrepancy between both the original information and the misinformation obtained from the partner. In other words, our methods are expected to be effective in terms of informational influence, as discussed above (Wright et al., 2009). If a person aware of discrepancies was notified of the sources of discrepancies before the individual memory test, there is no reason why they should provide responses in line with the misinformation in that test. On the other hand, if a person who did not discover the discrepancies is notified of possible discrepancies, they do not know what they should avoid. Thus, we expect that effectiveness of our methods will be higher among people aware of discrepancies between the original information and misinformation than among those unaware of such discrepancies.

issues.subcategory: Missing analysis plan for discrepancy awareness
issues.description: Missing analysis plan for discrepancy awareness: The analysis plan does not specify how the stated expectation that interventions will be more effective among discrepancy-aware participants will be tested. Although the plan mentions coding discussed items as “disputed” or “non-disputed,” the confirmatory model is a $4 \times 2$ Group $\times$ Discussed/Non-discussed ANOVA, and no analysis is given that incorporates awareness or dispute status as a moderator. This leaves an important theory-derived prediction without a preregistered statistical test or a clear indication that it is only exploratory.

issues.subcategory: Extended warning unblinds the MORI manipulation
issues.description: Extended warning unblinds the MORI manipulation: The Extended warning condition appears to disclose the MORI manipulation by telling participants that the partner saw a different version of the movie and explaining the deception. That disclosure may be an intended “enlightenment” manipulation, but it means any reduction in conformity in this group could partly reflect explicit source-relevance information or task-demand effects rather than the same kind of general resistance process targeted by the Education and Demonstration/motivation conditions. This should be considered when interpreting comparisons among the three interventions and claims about real-world applicability.
issues.quote: In a typical experiment using the MORI technique there may be a lot of participants aware of the discrepancies i.e., who remember both given information from the movie and misinformation from the partner. As stated above, participants who noticed the discrepancies may doubt their own memories. As a result, in the individual memory test they may provide an incorrect answer (i.e., answer in line with information obtained from the partner instead of answer in line with own memories). Extended warning, informing that the partner actually saw a different version of the movie and informing why the deception was applied, should make the participants who are aware of discrepancies discard the consistency assumption and make them rely on their own correct memories.

issues.subcategory: Unmeasured theoretical boundary condition
issues.description: Unmeasured theoretical boundary condition: The protocol’s theoretical account centers on participants who remember both the movie detail and the partner’s conflicting report, and it even predicts stronger intervention effects among participants aware of discrepancies. However, the planned analyses do not appear to include a direct measure or planned test of discrepancy awareness/source memory. The aggregate discussed-versus-non-discussed ANOVA may still estimate the practical intervention effect, but null or weak effects would be difficult to interpret mechanistically if many participants were unaware of the relevant discrepancies.
issues.quote: Of course, all the above reasoning only applies in the case of participants who do remember the content of both sources (the movie and the information from the conversation partner). The existence of subjects who are fully aware of discrepancies between the original and post-event information yet still give wrong answers due to the lack of confidence in their own memories is well established

issues.subcategory: Seven Sins descriptions in Education section
issues.description: Seven Sins descriptions in Education section: Some of the brief descriptions of Schacter’s Seven Sins appear conceptually imprecise, especially where transience is framed as forgetting “as a result of new experiences” and absent-mindedness is framed mainly as a failed retrieval attempt caused by diverted attention. Because the education intervention is grounded in this taxonomy, the protocol should make clear that the participant-facing content accurately represents the intended memory-error categories.
issues.quote:
More precisely, in this training the participants received a piece of paper containing a description of the seven major memory errors listed by Schacter (1999) that is: (1) transience forgetting past events over time as a result of new experiences; (2) absent-mindedness - occurs when an attempt to evoke a memory fails because attention has been drawn to another activity; (3) blocking - inability to access previously
stored information (e.g., the "tip of the tongue" phenomenon); (4) misattribution - occurs when confusing the source of information; (5) suggestibility - the inclusion of erroneous information received from other sources in memories, e.g., a message from another person; (6) bias - modifying past events in memory so that they are consistent with the current judgments and needs of the individual due to the filtering of past events by the present knowledge; (7) persistence unwanted memories persistently return to a person, e.g., traumatic memories.

issues.subcategory: Construct overlap between Education and Warning
issues.description: Construct overlap between Education and Warning: There may be construct overlap between the Education and Extended warning conditions: the Seven Sins content includes suggestibility and misattribution, including erroneous information from another person, which could indirectly alert participants to the co-witness misinformation they just encountered. This does not make the conditions identical, but it may limit how cleanly any education-condition effect can be attributed to broad metacognitive education rather than an embedded warning-like component.

issues.subcategory: Unclear mechanism in Education about memory rationale
issues.description: Unclear mechanism in Education about memory rationale: The rationale for Education about memory is somewhat underdetermined in the MORI/IMP context: the passage links general memory-fallibility education and skepticism about one's own memories to resistance, but it does not fully explain why this would reduce reliance on the co-witness rather than reduce confidence in one's own originally encoded detail. The following caveat acknowledges this possible reversal, so the issue is mainly that the hypothesized positive mechanism remains less explicit than for the Extended warning.
issues.quote: More precisely, it has been assumed that the better the metacognitive abilities of an individual and their knowledge about the deficits of memory, the smaller their susceptibility to misinformation (Roebers, 2002). Also, awareness of weaknesses and skepticism about one's own memories can lead participants to better monitor the source of information and to better control responses (Koriat \& Goldsmith, 1996). Moreover, as claimed by O'Sullivan and Howe (1995), activation of metamemory should make people more resilient to misinformation. Thus, a participant who is aware that memory is sometimes fallible makes greater efforts to detect erroneous information, and this favors the detection of inconsistencies between the event and the misinformation.

issues.subcategory: Paradoxical role of self-skepticism
issues.description: Paradoxical role of self-skepticism: The phrase skepticism about one's own memories may pull against the proposed Education about memory mechanism in this social-conformity setting. Informational influence is described earlier as arising when participants weigh the co-witness as correct against themselves as wrong, so the rationale would be stronger if it distinguished accuracy-enhancing source monitoring from a general reduction in confidence in one's own recollection. The next paragraph recognizes this possible downside, so this is an ambiguity in the stated mechanism rather than a settled contradiction.
issues.quote: Also, awareness of weaknesses and skepticism about one's own memories can lead participants to better monitor the source of information and to better control responses (Koriat \& Goldsmith, 1996). Moreover, as claimed by O'Sullivan and Howe (1995), activation of metamemory should make people more resilient to misinformation.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction regarding discrepancy detection
issues.description: Contradiction regarding discrepancy detection: The discrepancy-detection mechanism is underspecified here. Because the intervention is administered after collaborative recall and the framework emphasizes participants who are already aware of discrepancies, it is not fully clear whether detection refers to retrospective source monitoring at the final test or to increasing awareness among participants who had not previously noticed the discrepancy. The former is plausible, but the passage could otherwise seem misaligned with the stated IMP-based boundary conditions.
issues.quote: Thus, a participant who is aware that memory is sometimes fallible makes greater efforts to detect erroneous information, and this favors the detection of inconsistencies between the event and the misinformation.

issues.subcategory: Unclear mechanism in Education about memory
issues.description: Unclear mechanism in Education about memory: The rationale for the Education about memory intervention leaves the proximal mechanism somewhat underspecified. The text acknowledges that emphasizing memory fallibility could reduce confidence and increase conformity, but then predicts that the lecture may enhance monitoring, memory efficacy, or affect without specifying which component is expected to change, in what direction, or why the conformity-reducing route should dominate.
issues.quote:
However, a caveat should be mentioned here: presenting participants with research confirming the fallibility of memory may result in decreased confidence in their own memory, which, in turn, might result in increased suggestibility. Obviously, this was not the case in research by Szpitalak et al. (2019) in the context of the classic misinformation effect, but it is still possible in the proposed experiment. If this is the case, increased memory conformity is possible.

In the present study, as Szpitalak et al. (2019), we plan to use a presentation of the Seven Sins of Memory, but additionally we will familiarize the participants with more information about the mechanisms of memory. In particular, basic ideas about the constructive nature of memory and memory gaps will be presented and illustrated with examples. In addition, we will introduce participants to the concept of metamemory understood as knowledge about memory and awareness of it (Flavell, 1971). Hultsch, Hertzog, Dixon and Davidson (1988) identified four broad aspects of metamemory: (1) knowledge about memory processes, (2) memory monitoring, (3) sense of memory efficacy, and (4) memory-related affect. The planned lecture on memory functioning refers to the first of these aspects: we expect that it will increase the participants' knowledge about memory processes. We assume that the lecture will also enhance memory monitoring, sense of memory efficacy or even memory-related affect.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory claim regarding memory efficacy
issues.description: Contradictory claim regarding memory efficacy: There seems to be an issue with the claim that the lecture will “enhance” sense of memory efficacy or memory-related affect. Because the intervention emphasizes the constructive nature of memory, memory gaps, and the Seven Sins of Memory, its expected effects on efficacy and affect are ambiguous and could plausibly be negative or better calibrated rather than simply enhanced.
issues.quote: In particular, basic ideas about the constructive nature of memory and memory gaps will be presented and illustrated with examples. In addition, we will introduce participants to the concept of metamemory understood as knowledge about memory and awareness of it (Flavell, 1971). Hultsch, Hertzog, Dixon and Davidson (1988) identified four broad aspects of metamemory: (1) knowledge about memory processes, (2) memory monitoring, (3) sense of memory efficacy, and (4) memory-related affect. The planned lecture on memory functioning refers to the first of these aspects: we expect that it will increase the participants' knowledge about memory processes. We assume that the lecture will also enhance memory monitoring, sense of memory efficacy or even memory-related affect.

issues.subcategory: Missing ability component in Demonstration rationale
issues.description: Missing ability component in Demonstration rationale: The Demonstration and motivation rationale would be stronger if it clarified what, in the planned procedure, corresponds to the diagnostic “ability” component attributed to Sagarin et al. The proposed manipulation clearly includes a fallibility demonstration and motivational exhortation, but it is less clear whether it teaches participants a criterion for distinguishing legitimate from illegitimate influence in the co-witness setting.
issues.quote: The third method of reducing suggestive influence in the context of memory conformity is called Demonstration and motivation. In essence, it consists of two elements: (1) directly demonstrating the fallibility of memory to the participants, and (2) motivating them to provide correct answers by stressing how important it is to provide correct answers based on their own memory. This was inspired by existing research on resisting social influence presented by Sagarin, Cialdini, Rice, \& Serna (2002). Their technique was based on the inoculation theory, introduced by McGuire (1964). The theory and the technique consist of two elements: (1) demonstrating individual vulnerability to influence; (2) motivating participants to resist influence by teaching them to distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate influences. More precisely, the first of these elements is based on the premise that most people believe that social influence methods work for others but that they themselves are resistant to these methods. Thus, the demonstration of vulnerability to influence can break through the illusion of invulnerability, thereby increasing the vigilance of the individual. In an experiment conducted by Sagarin et al. (2002), such a demonstration consisted of introducing participants to an advertisement containing spurious experts.

issues.subcategory: DRM rationale in Demonstration and motivation
issues.description: DRM rationale in Demonstration and motivation: The theoretical link between the DRM component and reduced co-witness conformity is somewhat under-specified. The DRM exercise demonstrates associative false recall rather than the specific social/source-competition process in the MORI task; without a clearer mechanism, the demonstration could plausibly reduce confidence in participants' own memory even though the motivational component pushes them to rely on it.
issues.quote: We adapted the ideas from the research described above in the hope that it may be useful in mitigating memory conformity. The demonstration of the fallibility of memory will be done by means of the DRM technique (see detailed description below); the motivational aspect will be achieved by a podcast (i.e., only with sound; no visual material will be included) explaining how harmful a situation is in which one witness reports details that they do not actually remember but which were heard from other witnesses. Demonstrating the individual fallibility of memory should make the participants alert to the real possibility that their reports may be distorted as a result of a discussion with the partner. Participants aware of the fact that even very subtle influence may have an impact on memory functioning may reject the erroneous information provided by their partners more effectively. The motivational element of the procedure should furthermore increase the tendency to rely on one's own recollections.

issues.subcategory: Confounding effect of the DRM task on retention interval
issues.description: Confounding effect of the DRM task on retention interval: The Demonstration and motivation condition may be confounded with non-specific task differences because it adds an active DRM memory task before the final test, whereas the other conditions appear to involve only podcasts. Unless duration and cognitive load are matched or otherwise accounted for, differences in conformity or accuracy could partly reflect extra delay, interference, or fatigue rather than the intended demonstration-and-motivation mechanism.
issues.quote: The demonstration of the fallibility of memory will be done by means of the DRM technique (see detailed description below); the motivational aspect will be achieved by a podcast (i.e., only with sound; no visual material will be included) explaining how harmful a situation is in which one witness reports details that they do not actually remember but which were heard from other witnesses.

issues.subcategory: Replication power target in Section 2.1
issues.description: Replication power target in Section 2.1: The replication power analysis should identify the analysis population for the basic memory-conformity test. Because the interventions are administered before the final individual memory test, a discussed-vs.-non-discussed comparison across all four groups would combine the untreated conformity effect with any intervention effects; if the intended replication rests on the control group, the relevant $N$ is the control-group sample rather than the total sample.
issues.quote: With regard to replication of the memory conformity effect, the research design consists in a within-subjects manipulation: comparing the correctness of answers to the questions concerning the discussed details (related to misinformation) with the correctness of answers to the questions concerning the non-discussed (control) details. Technically, a repeated-measures ANOVA will be used to analyze the data. The calculation of the necessary sample size may be based on existing results in which the same procedure as that planned in the proposed study was used on a representative Polish sample. The existing results as regards effect sizes are Hedges' $\mathrm{g}=1.92, \mathrm{~N}=55$ (Ito et al., 2019) and Hedges' $\mathrm{g}=0.38, \mathrm{~N}=74$ (Kękuś et al., 2020).

issues.subcategory: Dyadic dependence in Section 2.1 power analysis
issues.description: Dyadic dependence in Section 2.1 power analysis: The power analysis for the intervention effect appears to treat individual participants as independent units, but the procedure assigns pairs to conditions and creates misinformation exposure through dyadic interaction. The justification should account for the dyadic unit of randomization and possible within-pair dependence, or state why these features do not materially affect the planned group-by-discussion interaction test.
issues.quote: The second aim of this study is to establish the efficacy of the three methods of reducing the memory conformity effect. There will be four groups of participants: three for each of the methods, and a control condition. Technically, detecting the efficacy of the methods consists in analyzing the interaction of the between-subjects factor (the groups) and the within-subjects factor (accuracy on discussed vs. non-discussed items): the impact of misinformation should be relatively lower in the three 'protected' groups than in the control one. Thus, the power analysis consists in finding the required sample size for an interaction in a two-factor ANOVA: the first factor is between-subjects; the second is within-subjects.

issues.subcategory: Violation of independence assumption in ANOVA
issues.description: Violation of independence assumption in ANOVA: The planned two-factor ANOVA treats 240 individual participants as independent observations even though participants are tested in interacting dyads and pairs are assigned to conditions. The analysis and power calculation should account for dyad-level dependence, for example through a dyad random effect, cluster-robust approach, or dyad-level aggregation; otherwise the degrees of freedom and standard errors for group and interaction tests may be too optimistic if within-dyad responses are correlated.
issues.quote: Technically, detecting the efficacy of the methods consists in analyzing the interaction of the between-subjects factor (the groups) and the within-subjects factor (accuracy on discussed vs. non-discussed items): the impact of misinformation should be relatively lower in the three 'protected' groups than in the control one. Thus, the power analysis consists in finding the required sample size for an interaction in a two-factor ANOVA: the first factor is between-subjects; the second is within-subjects.

issues.subcategory: Uncorrected alpha in power analysis for comparisons
issues.description: Uncorrected alpha in power analysis for comparisons: The follow-up comparison plan is underspecified with respect to multiplicity. The reported power for two-group comparisons appears to assume an unadjusted alpha; if pairwise comparisons among all four groups are intended with familywise error control, the required sample size and claimed sensitivity for those comparisons would be lower than stated.
issues.quote: For the planned comparisons between two groups, which will be necessary if the general interaction is significant, the required sample sizes are 492,82 , and 34 participants, respectively. Comparisons among all groups and non-directional significance tests are assumed.

issues.subcategory: Dyadic dependence in power and design sections
issues.description: Dyadic dependence in power and design sections: The sample-size justification and planned design appear not to account for dyadic clustering. Because participants are randomized in pairs and influence one another during the collaborative recall phase, treating $N=240$ individuals as independent in the power analysis or ANOVA could overstate precision; the inferential unit and error structure for participant-within-dyad observations should be specified.
issues.quote:
Considering the accessible financial, organizational and time resources, a sample of 240 participants was assumed; this allows for excellent power to detect medium and large effect sizes but not small ones.

### 2.2. Participants

The sample size will be set at 240 people ( 120 pairs). The participants enrolled in the study will be $16-35$ years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet. The age of the participants will be restricted in order to avoid a situation in which a very young participant would discuss the original material with an elderly one, which would possibly activate some confounding factors (e.g., Gabbert et al., 2004). In addition, the age of the participants in each pair will be matched as far as possible.

### 2.3. Design

In the study, the memory conformity effect will be measured in a within-subjects design and discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced. The correctness of answers to questions concerning discussed and non-discussed details will be compared. Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) Extended warning, (2) Education about memory, (3) Demonstration and motivation, and (4) control condition.

issues.subcategory: Confounding retention intervals across conditions
issues.description: Confounding retention intervals across conditions: The intervention phase may introduce unequal retention intervals across conditions. Extended warning and Education are described as approximately 7-minute podcasts, whereas Demonstration and motivation includes a DRM task plus a motivational podcast, and the control podcast duration is not specified. If the final memory test occurs immediately after each condition ends, group differences could partly reflect elapsed time since collaborative recall rather than intervention content.
issues.quote: First, in order to demonstrate to participants that they are vulnerable to influence, a substantially shortened and simplified procedure based on the DRM paradigm will be used (Roediger \& McDermott, 1995). It will consist of the participants listening to experimenter presenting lists of words from a common category, e.g., nurse, sick, medicine, health, hospital, dentist, ill, patient, office, stethoscope, surgeon, clinic, cure.

issues.subcategory: Collaborative test may confound co-witness misinformation
issues.description: Collaborative test may confound co-witness misinformation: The collaborative recognition phase may make the source of post-event information partly ambiguous. If the five displayed alternatives for a critical question include both MORI versions, participants are exposed to the partner-consistent detail as a response option as well as through the partner's statement. This could complicate the interpretation of later partner-consistent answers on discussed items as specifically reflecting co-witness memory conformity rather than exposure to salient alternatives during the collaborative test.
issues.quote: After watching the video, the participants will be engaged in a filler task (solving logic puzzles) for 15 minutes. After that, in the second phase, the participants will complete the collaborative recognition test. This is a series of questions, thanks to which the participants will discuss half of the discrepant details included in the original material, thus leading to mutual misinformation. The test will comprise 12 questions, four of which refer to critical details (e.g., What color was Eric's cap?), with the other eight being control questions. Each question and its five possible responses will be displayed in a PowerPoint presentation for 60 seconds while participants discuss the answer. If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented. The discussion will be audio recorded.

issues.subcategory: Fixed 60-second discussion window risks contamination
issues.description: Fixed 60-second discussion window risks contamination: The fixed 60-second display could create opportunities for off-target discussion after a pair has resolved the current question. Because non-discussed critical details are the within-subject baseline, it is not clear how the protocol will prevent or handle cases in which participants spontaneously discuss those details during the collaborative phase; the audio recordings may be important for identifying any such contamination.
issues.quote: Each question and its five possible responses will be displayed in a PowerPoint presentation for 60 seconds while participants discuss the answer. If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented. The discussion will be audio recorded.

issues.subcategory: Unaddressed failure of the DRM manipulation
issues.description: Unaddressed failure of the DRM manipulation: There is a potential issue in the Demonstration and motivation condition: participants who recall no DRM critical lures will not receive the intended personal demonstration that their own memory was distorted. The plan notes that DRM performance will be used as an exploratory predictor, but it remains unclear how the absence of false recall in this intervention will affect interpretation of the manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants in the DRM group will be given the DRM procedure with feedback, described above, which usually results in most of the participants falsely recalling a few of the critical lures. At this moment in this group, the experimenter will give the following information to the participants: "Thank you for completing this memory task. Please take a look at your sheets now. See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief. If so, you were fooled. These words are strongly associated with the sets I read, but they were not included in them. You can see how easily human memory can be distorted".

issues.subcategory: Post-intervention exclusions risk selection bias
issues.description: Post-intervention exclusions risk selection bias: The suspicion-based exclusion is post-randomization and post-intervention. Because the interventions themselves may increase awareness of misinformation or deception, excluding participants who guess the hypotheses could condition the analysis on a treatment-induced variable and alter comparability across groups, especially if exclusion rates differ between the intervention and control conditions.
issues.quote: Next, the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. If any of the participants correctly guesses our hypotheses, they will be excluded from the analysis and replaced with another person in order to maintain the correct sample size. We realize that this may result in more exclusion in the three experimental groups than in the control group; however, this seems to be less important than potential problems arising from analyzing results from participants who realized that they are being misled.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory exclusion criteria for the warning group
issues.description: Contradictory exclusion criteria for the warning group: The exclusion rule is especially problematic for the Extended warning condition. That intervention tells participants about the discrepancy/deception, while the exclusion rationale targets participants who realized that they were being misled. As written, the protocol does not distinguish awareness produced by the warning manipulation from prior suspicion or spontaneous hypothesis guessing.

The proposal focuses heavily on reducing co-witness misinformation, yet the proposed confirmatory estimand and statistical model do not currently match the core phenomenon being tested. The central outcome of interest is not simply lower overall accuracy on "discussed" versus "non-discussed" items; rather, it is the item-level adoption of partner-provided misinformation after participants are actually exposed to it.

Currently, the proposed two-factor ANOVA in Section 3 collapses across correct, misinformation-consistent, other, and total responses. It also includes discussed items on which the partner may not have actually supplied misinformation, and it ignores repeated observations, participants nested in dyads, and item-level variability across the eight critical details. An apparently critical issue is that the planned interaction could reflect varying item difficulty, willingness to answer, guessing, non-exposure, or dyad-specific influence rather than reduced conformity. Specifying a primary conformity estimand—such as misinformation-consistent responding on exposed critical items—and analyzing it with an item-level model that accounts for participant/dyad and item structure alongside preregistered contrasts might provide a much stronger foundation for the claims.


**Condition isolation and causal claims**

A central structural challenge for the experimental design is that the intervention conditions are not sufficiently isolable or matched to support precise causal claims about the three proposed mechanisms. As outlined, the "Extended warning" condition includes memory education, source-monitoring advice, confidence-related material, and explicit enlightenment that the partner saw a different version. Furthermore, "Education about memory" also teaches memory fallibility, while "Demonstration and motivation" combines a DRM task, personalized feedback, forensic consequences, and direct instruction not to rely on the partner.

In contrast, the control podcast on soft skills is not matched for forensic relevance, memory content, demand, arousal, suspicion, or experimenter interaction. The DRM condition also appears longer and more interactive than the podcast conditions. While there is a brief acknowledgement of overlap at the end of Section 1.1.4, this does not readily resolve the causal attribution problem. As the design stands, readers might attribute any observed condition differences to demand characteristics, treatment intensity, or explicit disclosure rather than the theorized active ingredients.


**Measuring discrepancy awareness**

Sections 1.1.1–1.1.4 repeatedly state that the interventions should work mainly for participants who remember both the movie detail and the partner’s conflicting detail, detect the discrepancy, and then intentionally choose whether to trust themselves or their partner. However, the mechanism foregrounded here—discrepancy awareness and informational influence—does not seem to be directly measured.

The current design measures final answers and confidence. The "disputed/non-disputed" discussion coding in Section 3 captures overt disagreement during collaboration, but it does not capture whether a participant internally noticed the discrepancy or later attributed an answer to the film or the discussion. Without item-level discrepancy-awareness or source-monitoring measures, the proposed theoretical interpretation remains largely post hoc. Because this protocol acts as a Stage 1 design, the preregistration of open-ended response coding requires substantial precision.
